This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Call a set $S\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ admissible if $(a,b)=1$ for all $a\neq b\in S$. Let\[G(n) = \max_{S\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}} \sum_{a\in S}a\]and\[H(n)=\sum_{p<n}p+ n\pi(n^{1/2}).\]Is it true that\[G(n) >H(n)-n^{1+o(1)}?\]Is it true that, for every $k\geq 2$, if $n$ is sufficiently large then the admissible set which maximises $G(n)$ contains at least one integer with at least $k$ prime factors?
#879: [Er84e][Er98]
number theory
Erdős and Van Lint proved that\[H(n)-n^{3/2-o(1)}<G(n)<H(n)\]and\[\frac{H(n)-G(n)}{n}\to \infty.\]They proved that $G(n)>H(n)-n^{1+o(1)}$ assuming 'plausible (but hopeless) assumptions about the distribution of primes'. They also prove the second claim when $k=2$.
See also [878].

 I have posted a Lean formalization and proof concerning the second part of Erdős Problem 879 to Formal Conjectures:
“Is it true that, for every k ≥ 2, if n is sufficiently large, an admissible set which maximises G(n) contains at least one integer with at least k distinct prime factors?”
FC: Formal Conjectures PR #5302
GitHub: erdos-879-lean
Lean4Web: standalone Lean4Web proof
The Lean proof gives a negative answer by disproving the statement for k = 3.
AI disclosure: This formalization and repository packaging were developed with assistance from OpenAI Codex and ChatGPT Astra.

 I would like to report some computational evidence concerning the case \(k=3\).
For a squarefree integer \(r\leq n\), define\[
 w_n(r)=\max\{m\leq n:\operatorname{rad}(m)=r\}.
\]Thus, once a radical \(r\) is chosen, the best representative is the largest
integer \(m\leq n\) having that radical.
With this notation, \(G(n)\) is the value of the following \(0\)-\(1\) integer
programme:\[
 \max \sum_r w_n(r)x_r,
\]subject to\[
 \sum_{r:p\mid r}x_r\leq 1
 \qquad (p\leq n\ \text{prime}),
\]where\[
 x_r\in\{0,1\}.
\]Here \(r\) ranges over all radicals occurring among integers \(m\leq n\). The
radical \(r=1\) is harmless: it is unconstrained and is always selected.
Indeed, replacing any chosen integer by the largest integer with the same
radical preserves admissibility and weakly increases the objective. The
constraints simply express the condition that no prime may divide two chosen
radicals.
Let \(G_{\leq 2}(n)\) denote the value of the same optimization problem, but with
the additional restriction\[
 \omega(r)\leq 2.
\]Thus \(G_{\leq 2}(n)\) is the best value obtainable using only integers with at
most two distinct prime factors, namely prime powers and numbers of the form
\(p^a q^b\). If\[
 G(n)=G_{\leq 2}(n),
\]then there exists an optimal admissible set containing no integer with three
distinct prime factors. Of course, this does not exclude the possibility that
other optimal sets may contain such integers.
The exact algorithm used was as follows.
Given \(n\) and \(t\in\{2,\infty\}\), initialize \({\cal R}=\emptyset\). For each
\(m=1,\ldots,n\), compute\[
 r=\operatorname{rad}(m).
\]If \(t=2\) and \(\omega(r)>2\), discard \(m\). Otherwise, for each radical
\(r\), retain only the largest integer \(m\leq n\) with that radical; call this
value \(w(r)\). Then solve\[
 \max \sum_{r\in{\cal R}} w(r)x_r
\]subject to\[
 \sum_{\substack{r\in{\cal R}\\ p\mid r}}x_r\leq 1
 \qquad(p\leq n\ \text{prime}),
\]with\[
 x_r\in\{0,1\}.
\]The case \(t=\infty\) gives \(G(n)\), while the case \(t=2\) gives
\(G_{\leq 2}(n)\).
The computations were carried out with the assistance of ChatGPT 5.5, which was
used to formulate and run the integer-programming calculations and to help check
the resulting values.
The exact computations give\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
n & G(n) & G_{\leq 2}(n) & G(n)-G_{\leq 2}(n)\\
\hline
20 & 98 & 98 & 0\\
50 & 445 & 445 & 0\\
100 & 1355 & 1355 & 0\\
200 & 5104 & 5104 & 0\\
500 & 24914 & 24914 & 0\\
1000 & 85684 & 85684 & 0\\
2000 & 302545 & 302545 & 0\\
5000 & 1636900 & 1636900 & 0\\
10000 & 5972789 & 5972789 & 0\\
20000 & 21825994 & 21825994 & 0
\end{array}
\]Thus, for every tested value of \(n\leq 20000\), the full optimum is already
attained within the subfamily of integers having at most two distinct prime
factors. In particular, although integers with three or more distinct prime
factors are available, they do not improve the optimum in these computations.
This is only finite computational evidence, and therefore not a disproof of any
eventual statement. However, it suggests the possible counter-conjecture\[
 G(n)=G_{\leq 2}(n)
\]for infinitely many \(n\), perhaps even for every \(n\). Equivalently, the
weighted matching problem using only prime powers and two-prime radicals may
already be strong enough to absorb all possible gains from using radicals with
three or more distinct prime factors.
